verdict.rationale: Two claims must be separated. That humanity is sinful from birth, before any moral act, is densely and pan-canonically attested. Ps 51:7 Hebrew (English 51:5) reads be-awon cholalti, with cholalti a Polal (passive) perfect, I was brought forth in iniquity, and u-be-chet yechemathni immi, in sin my mother conceived me. Job 14:4 denies by rhetorical question that a clean (tahor) can come from an unclean (tame). Gen 8:21 grounds the inclination, yetser lev ha-adam ra mi-ne'urav, evil from youth. Eph 2:3 calls the prior state phusei tekna orges, by nature children of wrath. Rom 5:14 has death reigning even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam, and 5:19 says kathistemi (aorist passive, constituted, appointed) the many sinners through one disobedience. That much is decisive. But the precise mechanism the stem encodes, an inherited corruption descending and shared from Adam as distinct from imputed guilt or merely transmitted inclination, is lexically underdetermined, because the crux clause eph ho pantes hemarton in Rom 5:12 admits multiple grammatical construals and phusis carries several attested senses.

scripture.force: The Hebrew (verse 7 in the Hebrew numbering) reads be-awon cholalti u-be-chet yechemathni immi. The verb cholalti is the root chul in the Polal stem, a passive intensive perfect first singular, I was brought forth, so the speaker is the object of the birthing, not the agent. The paired clause has his mother as subject, yechemathni, she conceived me, in chet (sin). The two prepositional phrases with the bet of circumstance locate iniquity and sin at the moment of gestation and birth, before any personal act. Hebrew poetic intensification pairs the two lines. What the words do NOT specify is whether the iniquity is the speaker's own inherited condition or a description of the sinful environment of conception. The dominant reading takes it as the speaker's native condition.

mi yitten tahor mi-tame lo echad. A rhetorical question, who can give a clean thing out of an unclean, answered no one (lo echad). The interrogative mi plus the negation frames a categorical impossibility, applied in context to one born of woman (compare Job 15:14, Job 25:4). The terms tahor and tame are the cultic clean and unclean vocabulary, here extended to human descent. The verse asserts that uncleanness propagates through generation but does not by itself define the uncleanness as guilt versus moral corruption.

ki yetser lev ha-adam ra mi-ne'urav. The noun yetser (inclination, frame, formed thing) construct with lev (heart) is said to be ra (evil) from youth. yetser is rare (nine occurrences) but here clearly names a settled disposition of the human heart from early life, paralleled in Gen 6:5 where every yetser of the thoughts of the heart is only ra all the day. This grounds the from-origin inclination, though yetser denotes disposition rather than imputed legal liability.

di' henos anthropou he hamartia eis ton kosmon eiselthen, kai dia tes hamartias ho thanatos, kai houtos eis pantas anthropous ho thanatos dielthen, eph ho pantes hemarton. The agency phrase dia plus genitive locates sin's entry through one man, and the consecutive houtos with the universalizing eis pantas establishes propagation of death to all. The crux is the closing eph ho pantes hemarton. The relative pronoun phrase eph ho is read at least three ways, causal (because all sinned), relative or consecutive (with the result that all sinned), or, taking ho as masculine referring back to the one man, in whom all sinned. The aorist hemarton (all sinned) is a completed past act. The Greek itself does not rank these construals, which is why the mechanism of transmission is contested at the text level even though the entry through one man is plain.

ebasileusen ho thanatos apo Adam mechri Mouseos kai epi tous me hamartesantas epi to homoiomati tes parabaseos Adam. Death reigned from Adam to Moses even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression. The participle phrase tous me hamartesantas (those not having sinned) in that specific manner is the strongest single clause against a pure personal-imitation reading, because it shows death (the wage of sin) extending to those who had no Adamic-style command to break. This implies a liability not grounded in their own equivalent act. It still does not, by lexis alone, decide between inherited guilt and inherited corruption as the ground.

di' henos paraptomatos eis pantas anthropous eis katakrima. The forensic noun katakrima (condemnation, only three NT occurrences, all in Romans at 5:16, 5:18, 8:1) plus the universalizer pantas anthropous entail that the one trespass yields a condemnation reaching all. The parallel structure (as through one, so to all) carries the corporate movement. The verse is the clearest single statement that the verdict reaches all through one.

dia tes parakoes tou henos anthropou hamartoloi katestathesan hoi polloi. The verb kathistemi, here aorist passive katestathesan (were constituted, were appointed), is across its 22 canon occurrences a verb of placing into an office or state (set over a household in Matt 24:45 and 25:21 and 23, appointed in Acts 6:3 and 7:10 and 7:27 and 7:35 and Titus 1:5 and Heb 5:1 and 7:28, rendered or made in Jas 3:6 and 4:4 and 2Pet 1:8). It is not an iterative verb of repeated behaviour. So the many were placed into the category sinner through the disobedience of the one, which resists a reduction to mere imitation. The verb names the result, not the mechanism.

emetha tekna phusei orges hos kai hoi loipoi. The dative phusei (by nature) modifies the predicate children of wrath, and the imperfect emetha (we were) names a prior shared state, with hos kai hoi loipoi (as also the rest) universalizing it. The force toward a native, pre-volitional standing is real. But phusis across its 14 NT uses carries several senses: birth-origin or natural endowment (Gal 2:15 Jews by nature, Rom 2:27 uncircumcision by nature, Rom 11:21 and 24 natural branches), kind or species (Jas 3:7), the regular order of things (1Cor 11:14 nature teaches, Rom 1:26 natural use), and essential constitution (2Pet 1:4 divine nature). Because phusei in Eph 2:3 can mean by birth-origin or in our essential condition as we then were, it strongly supports a native wrath-status but does not by the word alone fix it as a corruption descending specifically from Adam.

ontas nekrous tois paraptomasin kai tais hamartiais. The participle ontas (being) names a state of spiritual death in trespasses and sins prior to grace. The condition is described as already the readers' standing, the backdrop against which 2:4-5 sets God's action of making alive. It describes the depth of the fallen state but says nothing directly about its descent from Adam.

The wicked are estranged from the womb (me-rechem), they go astray from birth (mi-beten) speaking lies. The from-womb and from-birth idioms reinforce the pan-OT pattern of sin predating personal moral capacity. It is poetic and describes a class (the wicked) rather than asserting a universal anthropology, so it corroborates rather than carries the verdict.

complicating_texts.resolution: The closing clause eph ho pantes hemarton is the genuine lexical crux. The relative phrase eph ho is read causally (because all sinned), consecutively (so that all sinned), or with ho referring to the one man (in whom all sinned), and the aorist hemarton (all sinned) is a completed past. The causal reading favours a personal-sin ground, the in-whom reading favours inherited guilt. The from-birth verdict survives either reading because 5:14 (death over those who did not sin Adam's way) and 5:19 (kathistemi, were constituted sinners) carry an inherited liability independently of this clause, but the precise mechanism the proposition encodes is left open by the Greek.

The son shall not bear the iniquity (ba-awon) of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son. This governs judicial liability for personal acts within the covenant community, the level of who is punished in human and covenantal adjudication, not a universal anthropology of origin. It uses the same root awon as Ps 51:5 but in a courtroom sense. It limits how inherited corruption may be framed (it cannot mean a son is punished for the father's specific deeds in covenant law) without overturning the from-birth pattern of Rom 5 and the Psalms.

Fathers shall not be put to death for children, nor children for fathers, every man for his own sin. Same judicial-practice horizon as Ezek 18:20. It constrains human courts. It does not address the federal or natural solidarity claim in the Pauline eis pantas anthropous arc, which operates at the level of universal standing before God rather than penal procedure.

Gentiles do by nature (phusei) the things of the law. This shows the same word phusei used in Eph 2:3 can denote ordinary natural endowment or instinct rather than a corrupt condition, which is exactly why phusei in Eph 2:3 cannot by itself fix the by-nature wrath-status as a corruption descending from Adam as opposed to a description of the universal fallen condition. It is addressed by noting that context, not the word phusis alone, carries the sense in each place.

variant_units_examined.note: Witnesses vary between hymon (your) and hemon (our) and presence of the pronoun. The lexical pattern that the readers were nekrous (dead) in trespasses survives every reading, so the corruption claim is untouched.

This is a construal and translation divergence, not a manuscript split. All extant Greek witnesses read eph ho. The ambiguity is grammatical and lexical, not text-critical. The from-birth verdict rests on 5:14, 5:18, and 5:19 independently, so verdict impact is minor and the mechanism, not the verdict, is what the ambiguity unsettles.

variants.note: All anchor verses are in Psalms, Job, Genesis, Romans, and Ephesians, outside the ingested ECM window (3 John 1.1 to 1.15). No CBGM apparatus was examined and none is in scope for this verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads Ps 51:5 (cholalti, brought forth in iniquity), Job 14:4 (no clean from unclean), and Gen 8:21 (yetser ra from youth) as locating a real corrupt condition in the line of generation, and Eph 2:3 phusei as the native sharing of that condition. On this lens the proposition's word corruption is exactly right and the from-birth language is its strongest ground.

Reads henos anthropou and eph ho (taken as in whom) in Rom 5:12 to 19 as a legal-representative arrangement whose paraptoma is reckoned to descendants, with katakrima (forensic condemnation) and katestathesan (aorist passive, were constituted) carrying judicial appointment rather than infused corruption. On this lens the inherited element is primarily guilt, and Rom 5:14 (death over non-Adamic-style sinners) is the key support.

Reads the OT material, especially Gen 6:5 and 8:21 yetser and Ps 58:3 from the womb, as teaching an inherited evil disposition or bent rather than either imputed legal guilt or total inability. This lens affirms a from-birth sinful inclination, which the proposition's phrase sinful nature can name, while remaining cautious about the stronger legal claim.

Treats Adam as humanity's archetypal head whose act shapes the corporate human situation, so that eis pantas anthropous expresses solidarity in a fallen order. Less precise on whether the link is legal or natural, but coheres with the universalizing pas language and with houtos (so) linking the one and the all.

Reads eph ho pantes hemarton causally (because all sinned) and treats the universality as the sum of individual sins after Adam's example, denying any inherited corruption or guilt. This lens has a real grammatical foothold in the causal construal of eph ho and in the aorist hemarton as completed personal acts. Its weakness is Rom 5:14, where death reigns over tous me hamartesantas, those who did not sin in Adam's manner, and the aorist passive katestathesan in 5:19, which names a constituting rather than a behaving. So the words press against a pure imitation reading without absolutely excluding a minimal version of it.

hermeneutics.notes: The from-birth, pre-volitional sinful condition is supported across four of five lenses and resists the fifth on the grammar of 5:14 and 5:19. The lenses divide not on whether the condition is innate but on its mechanism, imputed guilt versus transmitted corruption versus inherited inclination. The proposition bundles innate sinfulness with a specific descent-from-Adam corruption, and the vocabulary supports the first firmly while underdetermining the second.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Human beings come into existence already in a sinful condition that precedes their own moral acts, and this condition is connected to Adam and places them under divine wrath.
stem_audit.notes: The stem phrases inherited from Adam, sharing in his corruption import a specific transmission mechanism (a corruption descending by inheritance) into the proposition. The from-birth sinful condition and the by-nature wrath-status are lexically supported (Ps 51:7, Job 14:4, Gen 8:21, Ps 58:3, Eph 2:3 phusei, Rom 5:14, 5:18, 5:19), so affirms is kept true as in the prior file. Confidence is lowered from high to medium relative to the prior file because the queried lexis shows the mechanism the stem encodes is underdetermined: eph ho in Rom 5:12 admits causal, consecutive, and in-whom construals that the Greek does not rank, and phusis in Eph 2:3 carries multiple attested senses (birth-origin, kind, natural order, essential constitution), so the words do not by themselves fix inherited corruption as against imputed guilt or merely an inherited inclination. This is a confidence change driven by lexical findings, not an affirms change, so the verdict token is not flipped. The neutralized form states the supported core without preloading the contested mechanism.

lay_summary: Across the Hebrew and Greek texts, several writers describe humans as sinful from the very start, not only after later choices. In Psalm 51 the writer says he was brought forth in iniquity and that in sin his mother conceived him, and the verb for brought forth is a passive form, so he is the one being birthed into that condition. Job 14:4 asks who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean and answers no one. Genesis 8:21 says the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth, and Psalm 58:3 says the wicked go astray from the womb. In the New Testament Paul says in Romans 5 that through one man sin entered the world and death spread to all, and that death reigned even over people who had not broken a direct command the way Adam did, which only makes sense if some liability is carried rather than only earned. He also says that through one man's disobedience the many were constituted sinners, using a verb that elsewhere means to appoint or place into a position, not merely to behave badly. Ephesians 2 adds that we were by nature children of wrath, like everyone else. So the claim that people start out in a sinful condition, before their own acts, rests on dense, repeated words spanning the Psalms, Job, Genesis, and Paul. Where the text leaves room, and why thoughtful readers still differ, is the exact mechanism. The key Greek phrase in Romans 5:12, often rendered because all sinned, can also be read in whom all sinned or with the result that all sinned, and the grammar itself does not settle which. The word translated by nature in Ephesians is also used elsewhere for ordinary natural instinct and for kind or species, so it shows a native condition but does not by itself prove a corruption passed down specifically from Adam as opposed to inherited guilt or an inherited bent. The from-birth sinfulness is firm. The precise way it descends is the part the words leave open.
